title: Self-Guided Low Light Object Detection Framework
claim: Auxiliary supervision branches used only during training can be dropped at test time, leaving the base model's inference cost unchanged.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; large training panel, small testing panel, dashed red loss links
description: The figure has two rounded panels. The large left panel, "Training Stage", shows a detector made of a backbone B and a head H, fed by an input image x. Hatched boxes and cubes mark the auxiliary pipeline: an enhancing module E, a denoising module D, Fourier transform circles F, two modules P and A, an inverse-Fourier fusion node F^-1, and a decoder G. The pipeline produces a fused target image x-hat and a decoded image x-tilde. A dashed red double arrow labelled L_self joins these two images. A dashed red arrow labelled L_det points into the head. The smaller right panel, "Testing Stage", shows only x → B → H → Output, with the auxiliary parts removed. A grey chevron links the two panels. The drawing is black and white with red accents on the losses.
caption: Overview of the proposed framework. We propose an auxiliary pipeline, depicted by dashed-line patterns, to generate a target image for self-guided supervision during training. This pipeline consists of a decoder (G), an enhancing module (E), a denoising module (D), and Fourierbased image fusion (F, F−1). At the testing stage, the auxiliary pipeline is removed, maintaining the original inference cost of the detector while improving its performance in low-light environments.
abstract: Object detection in low-light environments is inherently challenging due to limited contrast and heavy noise, both of which significantly degrade feature representations. In this paper, we propose a novel self-guided low-light object detection framework that effectively addresses these issues without introducing additional parameters or increasing inference time. Our method incorporates a detachable auxiliary pipeline during training, consisting of an image enhancement module and a denoising module, followed by a Fourier-domain fusion block. This pipeline improves the feature representation of the detector's backbone, enhancing its robustness under low-light conditions. Importantly, at inference time, our method incurs no additional computational cost compared to the baseline detector while achieving substantial performance improvements. Extensive experiments on widely used low-light object detection benchmarks, such as DARK FACE and ExDark, demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, experiments on the nuImages dataset show that our approach can outperform domain adaptation methods—especially when a large domain gap between source and target domains is inevitable in the real-world applications—highlighting its practical effectiveness. Code is available at https://github.com/gw-shin/SGLDet.
